clue.text: Cocaine? The bloke's son's game

parts.note: C is drug slang for cocaine
the bloke is 'he', so 'the bloke's' is HE'S

explanation.surface: A question about drugs, followed by the claim that some man's son plays at it.
explanation.walkthrough: C is slang shorthand for cocaine. The apostrophes are ignored: HE'S and S just join up.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is a board game played by two people with kings, queens and pawns.

clue.text: Country breathing apparatus misses onset of slaughter

indicators.note: the apparatus misses, or goes without, the letter named next

parts.note: scuba is the diver's self-contained underwater breathing apparatus

indicators.note: the onset of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of slaughter

explanation.surface: A country whose diving gear fails just as a massacre begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is an island nation in the Caribbean, a country in its own right.

clue.text: It's pointless going green, convulsing and getting an erection

indicators.note: convulsing means writhing, so the letters of going green are thrown about

parts.note: a point is a compass point; being point-less, the pool loses one such letter, East

explanation.surface: Someone turning green and shaking while becoming aroused, a typically Private Eye picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointless' looks like a comment on the effort, but it strips one compass point, E, from the letters before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To engorge is to swell with blood, which is how an erection happens.

clue.text: Pitiful respect shown by Brenda's staff

indicators.note: pitiful means in a sorry state, so the word respect is shown in wretched disorder

explanation.surface: The Queen's servants show her only a grudging, pitiful deference.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so her staff is the royal rod, not her servants.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental rod a monarch holds as a symbol of sovereignty.

clue.text: Alternative live comic's caught out atrocious ex-president

indicators.note: an alternative version of the words gives the letters in another order
out tells us the letter for caught is taken away from the pool

explanation.surface: An alternative comedian, performing live, catches out a brutal former head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: C for caught comes from cricket scorecards. 'Alternative live comic' suggests a stand-up, but alternative is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Slobodan Milosevic, former president of Serbia and Yugoslavia, was tried for war crimes at The Hague.

clue.text: Head from this female supposedly made men rock hard

definitions.text: Head from this female supposedly made men rock hard

parts.words: Head from this female supposedly made men rock hard
parts.note: a Gorgon of Greek myth whose gaze, even from her severed head, turned men to stone; the surface is a smutty double entendre

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as sexual innuendo; the mythical reading is literal petrification.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend Perseus beheaded this Gorgon, and her head still turned onlookers into stone statues.

clue.text: Retriever of party, Reverend Blair finally curbing agitation

parts.note: Lab is short for the Labour Party

indicators.note: curbing means hemming in, so the two letters enclose the word for agitation

parts.note: R. is an abbreviation for Reverend

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of Blair

parts.note: the last letter of Blair
ado is fuss or agitation

explanation.surface: A party dog for the Labour leader, with Blair, cast as a vicar, calming a commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye cast Tony Blair as 'the Reverend' in its parish-newsletter spoof, which is why Reverend and Blair sit together.
explanation.definitionFit: A Labrador is a breed of retriever, a gun dog bred to fetch shot game.

clue.text: "Go in for cleavage, Posh — start to pad bust"

definitions.note: a verb phrase: to separate into parts, which is what cleaving does

parts.note: to bust something is to split it
U means upper-class, posh

indicators.note: the start of pad is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of pad

explanation.surface: Advice to Posh Spice to enhance her cleavage by padding her bust.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh is Victoria Beckham, but here it gives U, the old label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleavage in its older sense is a division, so going in for it means to divide or separate.

clue.text: Topless woman a tabloid tipped as the star of the evening

indicators.note: topless means the head letter of the word is removed

parts.note: Eve, the first woman

indicators.note: tipped means tipped over, so the paper's name runs upward in this down entry

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A tabloid picks a topless model as the star of the night, Page Three style.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is famous for its topless Page Three models, which is the scene the surface paints.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus is the planet seen brightly after sunset, traditionally called the evening star.

clue.text: Something of the cheap and nasty about Nazi leader confiscating 'Look Back in —'

definitions.text: Something of the cheap and nasty

parts.note: C is circa, about

indicators.note: confiscating means taking in, so Hess's name holds the next letters

parts.note: Rudolf Hess was Hitler's deputy as leader of the Nazi Party

indicators.note: back means the word for look runs backwards

parts.note: to look is to see

explanation.surface: A dismissive review of something tacky, mentioning a Nazi and a gap in Osborne's play title.
explanation.walkthrough: Look Back in Anger is John Osborne's play; the dash invites ANGER, but only 'Look', 'Back' and 'in' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesiness is a quality of tackiness or naff, low-grade taste, the stuff of cheap and nasty things.

clue.text: The sort to boast "I give great oral sex"

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a conceited person who brags
second meaning: the jokey reading, 'I give the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is slang for oral sex, so the boast 'I give great head' becomes a big-head.
explanation.definitionFit: A bighead is an arrogant person full of self-importance, given to bragging about themselves.

clue.text: Blair's lot, suffering reverse, can change Environment no, to achieve stability

indicators.note: suffering a reverse means the abbreviation turns back to front

parts.note: Tony Blair's party, Labour, abbreviated Lab

indicators.note: change tells us the letters of can and the next letter are rearranged

parts.note: E is a standard abbreviation for environment

explanation.surface: Labour, after a setback, rethinks its green policy to steady itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To balance is to keep steady and in equilibrium, which is reaching stability.

clue.text: See 28
Like much of Asia, it means the earth in Sun circulation terms

parts.note: counting the planets circling the Sun, Earth is third
the world is the earth

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about Asia and what the earth means in solar orbits.
explanation.walkthrough: The earth is the third planet from the Sun, so in orbital terms it is 'third world'.
explanation.definitionFit: Third World was the term for developing countries, much of Asia among them in 2001.

clue.text: Cow showing extremes of foot and mouth that's destroyed with indecisive muttering

indicators.note: destroyed means these letters are broken up and reordered
the extremes of the phrase foot and mouth are its very first and very last letters

parts.note: its outer letters, one from each end of the phrase
i.e. is short for id est, that is
er is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: A cow with foot-and-mouth disease is culled while someone mumbles uncertainly.
explanation.definitionFit: A heifer is a young female bovine that has not yet borne a calf, a type of cow.

clue.text: Brenda's captivated by firm, erect and popular French scorer

indicators.note: captivated by means held by, so the Queen's letters sit within the others

parts.note: Co. is short for company, a firm
erect means standing up
in means fashionable, popular
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: The Queen swoons over a firm, upstanding and popular French goalscorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scorer' suggests a footballer, but here it is one who writes scores: a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: François Couperin was a French Baroque composer of harpsichord music, someone who wrote scores.

clue.text: Cardinal rule I concocted about single cult hero

indicators.note: about means the mixed letters go round the following ones
concocted means made up, so the letters of rule I are mixed

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one
Che Guevara, revolutionary turned poster cult hero

explanation.surface: A church's leading rule being devised around a single cult figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal rule' reads as one phrase, a principal law, but cardinal is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Richelieu was the 17th-century French cardinal and chief minister to Louis XIII.

clue.text: A yardie's ground, quite likely

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase; the answer is a phrase used to mean probably

indicators.note: ground means crushed and reduced, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A Jamaican gangster's patch, as one might guess.
explanation.walkthrough: A Yardie is a member of a Jamaican criminal gang; 'ground' looks like his territory.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I dare say' concedes that something is probably so, a way of granting likelihood.

clue.text: Kray-killing, apparently, is what put paid to Charles

parts.note: Reg (Reggie) Kray, one of the East End gangster twins
-icide is the word ending meaning a killing, as in homicide

explanation.surface: A Kray murder, it is suggested, was what finished off a Charles.
explanation.walkthrough: Reggie Kray and his twin Ronnie ran London's 1960s underworld, so killing Reg is jokily 'Reg-icide'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles I was executed in 1649, the killing of a king, which is what the word names.

clue.text: Vaulted to get away from frenzied copulator

indicators.note: get away from tells us the letters of to leave the pool
frenzied means wild, so the remaining letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone vaults over a wall to escape a sex-crazed pursuer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vaulted' looks like a verb, leaping, but it is an adjective: arched like a dome.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupolar describes something shaped like a cupola, a domed or arched roof.

clue.text: Testicles, er, cut out for flares, we hear

indicators.note: cut out means the letters of er are removed from the slang word

parts.note: knackers is British slang for testicles

explanation.surface: A man's testicles are snipped off, apparently to make room for flared trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on sound: flares said aloud is flairs, and a flair is a knack.
explanation.definitionFit: A knack is a natural aptitude, the same as a flair, which matches flares by sound.

clue.text: Like breasts holding one fast

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the word encloses the letter for one

parts.note: nipply jokily means nipple-like or having nipples

explanation.surface: Something breast-shaped clutching one item tightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like 'held fast', but it is the definition: quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy means quick and nimble, so doing something nippily is doing it swiftly.

clue.text: One continually making critical remarks about penis on royal

indicators.note: about means around, in disorder, so the letters of penis are rearranged

explanation.surface: A carping critic of a royal's private parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniper is a persistent fault-finder who takes potshots at others with snide criticism.

clue.text: Green, jumped-up sort demands a parliamentary enforcer for each paparazzo

parts.note: a whip keeps MPs voting with their party
per means for each
a snapper is a photographer, like a paparazzo

explanation.surface: An upstart Green politician wants a party whip for every celebrity photographer.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippersnapper is a young, inexperienced person who is presumptuous and overconfident, both callow and cocky.

clue.text: Popular bookkeepers, old people

parts.note: in means popular
CAs are chartered accountants, who keep books

explanation.surface: Accountants who are well liked, and also elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' reads as pensioners; it means a people of history.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the ancient Andean civilisation of Peru, a historical nation.

clue.text: Enthusiastic attempt-to get inside a girl's top

indicators.note: the attempt is placed inside the other letters
a word's top in a down entry is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of girl
a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: An eager try at getting inside a girl's blouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Agog means eagerly excited and full of keen anticipation.

clue.text: Volatile Clare Short's first — Labour leader having intervened — to get orders to return

indicators.note: the leader comes between letters, placed inside the anagram
unstable and changeable, so the letters shift about
the leading letter of the word is taken
the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Clare Short, the fiery Labour MP, with her party leader intervening.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare Short was a Labour cabinet minister. 'Volatile' rearranges CLARE into RECAL; 'having intervened' puts L (Labour's leader) inside it, and the S of Short follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall someone is to order them to come back, as with an ambassador.

clue.text: Getting off with someone generates interest in shaving

indicators.note: in means placed inside the word for shaving

parts.note: paring is shaving off thin layers
i is the abbreviation for interest in finance

explanation.surface: Hooking up with someone sparks an interest in personal grooming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting off with' is British slang for snogging or pulling someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Pairing up means forming a couple, which is what getting off with someone is.

clue.text: Stupid sod Terry Venable's second sub seeker

indicators.note: stupid means confused, so the letters are rearranged
the second letter of Venables

parts.note: the second letter of Venables

explanation.surface: An insult to football manager Terry Venables, who keeps looking for a substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: Terry Venables was England's football manager; 'sub' looks like a substitute but means a submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is a fast warship whose job includes hunting submarines.

clue.text: Tracey and other such exhibitionists strip for you in here

definitions.text: Tracey and other such exhibitionists strip for you in here

parts.words: Tracey and other such exhibitionists strip for you in here
parts.note: Tracey Emin and her contemporaries exhibited themselves and their lives; the group was dubbed after its members' youth and nationality

explanation.walkthrough: The exhibitionists are artists who exhibit, not people who undress; Tracey Emin famously displayed her own unmade bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The YBAs were the 1990s group of London artists including Tracey Emin and Damien Hirst.
